<reason>A won by controlling the motion's actual decision rule. Its core move — that B's German-style model achieves universality only by severing the access-to-work tie the motion condemns ("universal financing in an employer costume"; "plural payers strapped to single-payer scaffolding, minus the savings") — was pressed in every speech and never escaped, since every safeguard B cited (state backstops, no-refusal mandates, risk equalization) works by decoupling coverage from the job. A also kept an efficiency/bargaining-power route that B never engaged, and its refusal-symmetry answer (fund-switching "changes the letterhead on the rejection") blunted B's central exit argument without reply. B landed real blows: the earmark/firewall answer, the judo turning A's "track funding, not payer count" concession into a funding-defense question, and "a single number to squeeze." But B's path required reframing the motion into generic multi-payer vs. single-payer, its closing frame ("what single-payer uniquely adds") ignored A's live efficiency benefits, and the clipped second rebuttal was a genuine execution cost. Both were disciplined and rhetorically sharp; A left the cleaner, more motion-faithful route to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1–A2.3's recharacterization of B's exemplar countries as systems that work "precisely because they refuse to tie access to work status" defined the whole debate: B's answers (earmark, governance, plurality) showed the financing channel survives but conceded the access tie must be engineered away, which A converted into the closing's decisive crystallization — and B's silence on admin waste and on A's "letterhead on the rejection" symmetry point left those A routes live at the end.</best_rebuttal>
